name: Oldowan core-and-flake knapping
date_note: Gona, Ethiopia c.2.6 Ma; Lomekwi 3 (Kenya) c.3.3 Ma contested; persists alongside Acheulean
making_significance: Hominins struck sharp flakes from cobbles with a hammerstone, the earliest well-documented systematic tool-making.
free_sources: Smithsonian NMNH Anthropology via Smithsonian Open Access (CC0 where marked); Wikimedia Commons; open-access excavation reports
notes: Lomekwian (3.3 Ma) should be noted as contested earlier case.

name: Acheulean handaxe making
date_note: Kokiselei, West Turkana c.1.76 Ma; ends at different times regionally
making_significance: Knappers thinned a stone blank from both faces to a planned symmetrical form, showing a mental template carried over a million years.
leaves_out: Named after a French site though earliest examples are African.
free_sources: Smithsonian NMNH Anthropology via Smithsonian Open Access (CC0 where marked); Met Open Access (CC0); Wikimedia Commons; open-access excavation reports

name: Levallois prepared-core technique
date_note: first known c.400–300 ka; earlier claims contested
making_significance: Knappers shaped a core so that a flake of predetermined size and shape could be removed in one blow.
free_sources: Smithsonian NMNH Anthropology via Smithsonian Open Access (CC0 where marked); Wikimedia Commons; open-access excavation reports

name: Pressure flaking
date_note: Blombos Cave silcrete points c.75 ka (Mourre et al. 2010)
making_significance: Pushing a pointed tool against an edge (often of heat-treated stone) removes thin, controlled flakes, used for fine points such as Solutrean leaves, Egyptian ripple-flaked knives and Danish flint daggers.
free_sources: Smithsonian NMNH Anthropology via Smithsonian Open Access (CC0 where marked); Met Open Access (CC0); Wikimedia Commons

name: Microlith production and hafting
date_note: Pinnacle Point 5-6 c.71 ka; compound adhesives at Sibudu c.70 ka
making_significance: Small standardised stone inserts were glued or bound into wooden or bone shafts to make replaceable composite tools and weapons.
free_sources: Smithsonian NMNH Anthropology via Smithsonian Open Access (CC0 where marked); Wikimedia Commons; open-access excavation reports

name: Microblade technology
date_note: c.25 ka in Siberia and North China; in Alaska by c.14 ka
making_significance: Tiny parallel blades pressed from prepared cores were set into slotted bone and antler points, a toolkit carried into the Americas.
materials_techniques: pressure blade removal; slotted bone points
free_sources: open-access journal articles; Wikimedia Commons

name: Edge-ground and polished stone
date_note: edge-ground axe fragment, Carpenter's Gap, Australia c.46–44 ka (Hiscock et al. 2016); Japan c.38 ka; Neolithic polishing widespread later
making_significance: Grinding stone against abrasive sandstone and water produced durable edges and polished surfaces for axes, adzes and ornaments.
leaves_out: Early Australian date overturns a Europe-centred 'Neolithic' definition.
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); Smithsonian NMNH Anthropology via Smithsonian Open Access (CC0 where marked); Wikimedia Commons; Auckland Museum Online Collection (CC BY where marked)

name: Hardstone and jade working with abrasives
other_names: lapidary sawing and drilling of nephrite and jadeite
date_note: Xinglongwa jade earrings c.6200–5400 BCE; Olmec jadeite; Māori pounamu
making_significance: Because jade is too tough to carve, makers sawed, drilled and polished it with harder abrasive sand and string, bamboo or stone tools.
materials_techniques: string sawing; tubular drilling; abrasive polishing
functions: ritual and belief;rule and display;clothing and adornment
leaves_out: Pounamu is a taonga with protocols.
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access (CC0); National Palace Museum Taipei Open Data; Te Papa Collections Online (CC BY where marked; otherwise link out); Wikimedia Commons

name: Shell bead making
date_note: perforated Nassarius shells at Skhul (c.100–135 ka), Taforalt (c.82 ka) and Blombos (c.75 ka)
making_significance: Perforating and stringing small shells is among the oldest evidence of personal ornament and symbolic making.
free_sources: open-access journal articles; Wikimedia Commons

name: Ostrich eggshell bead making
date_note: c.50 ka in East Africa (earlier claims exist); ongoing among San and other makers
making_significance: Makers break, drill and grind ostrich eggshell into standard disc beads used in gift exchange over tens of thousands of years.
free_sources: British Museum EMKP (CC); Wikimedia Commons; open-access journal articles

name: Bone and antler working
date_note: Katanda barbed bone points (DR Congo) c.90 ka, dating debated; groove-and-splinter in Upper Palaeolithic Europe
making_significance: Makers split, ground and carved bone and antler into points, harpoons, needles and figures.
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); Wikimedia Commons; open-access excavation reports

name: Eyed-needle sewing
date_note: earliest reliable eyed needles c. 45–40 ka in Siberia (Strashnaya Cave 44–49 ka); the Denisova Cave claim of c. 50 ka rests on one radiocarbon date and most of layer 11 dates 25–20 ka; Mezmaiskaya (Caucasus) 36–28 ka
making_significance: The eyed needle allowed close-fitting sewn clothing, which made life in cold northern climates possible.
free_sources: open-access journal articles; Wikimedia Commons

name: Cordage and string twisting
date_note: three-ply cord fragment, Abri du Maras, France c.41–52 ka (Neanderthal)
making_significance: Twisting and plying plant fibres into string underlies nets, snares, bags, textiles and binding.
free_sources: open-access journal articles

name: Ochre and pigment processing
date_note: Blombos Cave ochre-processing kits c.100 ka; ochre use c.300 ka at Olorgesailie
making_significance: Grinding ochre and mixing it with binders in shell containers is among the earliest recipes for a manufactured material.
free_sources: open-access journal articles; Wikimedia Commons

name: Rock painting
date_note: Leang Karampuang, Sulawesi c.51 ka; Iberian hand stencils >64 ka contested; ongoing in some communities
making_significance: Painters applied ochre, charcoal and other pigments to rock by hand, brush, stencil and spray, in some places over tens of thousands of years.
materials_techniques: spray stencilling; brush painting; pigment mixing
leaves_out: Many sites are sacred to living communities.
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons; open-access excavation reports; community-published site

name: Rock engraving
date_note: engraved ochre, Blombos c.75 ka; Murujuga petroglyphs possibly >40 ka; engraved shell at Trinil c.500 ka contested
making_significance: Pecking, incising and abrading rock surfaces produced lasting images, from Murujuga to Tamgaly to Alta.
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons; UNESCO World Heritage / Intangible Cultural Heritage pages (link out); community-published site

name: Fire-setting (mining)
date_note: Rudna Glava copper mine, Serbia, 5th millennium BCE; used until the 19th c.
making_significance: Miners heated rock faces with fire so they cracked, then broke them with stone hammers to reach ore and flint.
free_sources: open-access excavation reports; Wikimedia Commons

name: Early fired-clay vessels
date_note: Xianrendong Cave, China c.20–19 ka BP; Japan c.16 ka; Ounjougou, Mali c.9400 BCE — invented several times
making_significance: Hunter-gatherers in East Asia and later in the Sahara made fired clay vessels independently, long before farming.
materials_techniques: coil or slab forming; open firing
leaves_out: Undoes the idea that pottery follows agriculture.
free_sources: open-access journal articles; Wikimedia Commons

name: Coil building
date_note: among the earliest and most widespread forming methods; ongoing
making_significance: Building vessels from rolled ropes of clay allows large and varied forms without a wheel, as in Pueblo, Nigerian and Papuan pottery.
leaves_out: Many coil traditions are women's practice.
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); Smithsonian NMNH Anthropology via Smithsonian Open Access (CC0 where marked); Wikimedia Commons

name: Paddle-and-anvil forming
date_note: ancient; ongoing
making_significance: Beating a clay form with a paddle against a stone or clay anvil held inside thins and shapes the wall.
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons; open-access journal articles

name: Press-moulding
date_note: moulded plaques in Mesopotamia early 2nd millennium BCE; Moche mould-made vessels 100–800 CE
making_significance: Pressing clay into fired moulds allowed repeated figures and vessels in series, as in Moche portrait vessels and Roman lamps.
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access (CC0); Wikimedia Commons

name: Potter's wheel throwing
date_note: slow wheel in Mesopotamia and Levant c.4500–3500 BCE; fast wheel later and debated; not used in pre-Hispanic Americas
making_significance: The rotating wheel allowed faster, thinner and more uniform vessels and often shifted pottery toward specialist workshops.
leaves_out: Wheel pottery is not a measure of 'advancement'; many societies chose not to adopt it.
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access (CC0); Wikimedia Commons

name: Slip casting
date_note: Staffordshire c.1740s with plaster-of-Paris moulds
making_significance: Pouring liquid clay into absorbent plaster moulds made thin, identical wares in quantity, a basis of industrial ceramics.
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); V&A collections (link out); Wikimedia Commons

name: Burnishing
date_note: ancient and widespread; ongoing (e.g. San Ildefonso blackware from 1918–19)
making_significance: Rubbing leather-hard clay with a smooth stone compacts and shines the surface without glaze, as in San Ildefonso blackware.
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); Smithsonian NMNH Anthropology via Smithsonian Open Access (CC0 where marked); Wikimedia Commons

name: Open firing
date_note: earliest firing method; ongoing
making_significance: Firing pots in an open bonfire or pit with fuel packed around them needs no kiln and is still used by many potters.
materials_techniques: bonfire; dung or wood fuel; smudging
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons; open-access journal articles

name: Updraft kiln
date_note: Halaf and Samarran kilns c.6000 BCE (e.g. Yarim Tepe); Yangshao kilns in China
making_significance: Separating the firebox from the ware chamber gave potters more even and higher temperatures than open firing.
free_sources: open-access excavation reports; Wikimedia Commons

name: Dragon kiln
date_note: proto-dragon kilns in Zhejiang in the Shang period; mature from Eastern Han
making_significance: Long sloping tunnel kilns built up hillsides reached stoneware temperatures and fired thousands of pieces at once.
free_sources: open-access journal articles; Wikimedia Commons

name: Anagama
date_note: introduced from Korea to Japan c.5th c. for Sue ware
making_significance: A single-chamber sloping tunnel kiln whose long wood firings leave natural ash glaze and flashing on the ware.
free_sources: ColBase Japan national museums (Japan Government Standard Terms); Met Open Access (CC0); Wikimedia Commons

name: Noborigama
date_note: Korean-derived chambered kilns in Karatsu c.1590s–1600s
making_significance: A stepped series of chambers up a slope reuses heat from one chamber to the next, raising output for stoneware and porcelain.
free_sources: ColBase Japan national museums (Japan Government Standard Terms); Met Open Access (CC0); Wikimedia Commons

name: Ash glaze
date_note: Shang proto-porcelain in southern China c.1500 BCE
making_significance: Wood ash, melting on or mixed into a glaze at high temperature, gives the earliest high-fired glazes in East Asia.
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access (CC0); ColBase Japan national museums (Japan Government Standard Terms)

name: Lead glaze
date_note: Roman lead-glazed wares and Han China c.2nd–1st c. BCE; Tang sancai 8th c.
making_significance: Lead-based glazes melt at low temperature and take bright copper greens, iron ambers and cobalt blues.
object_types: sancai figures; Roman glazed cups; slipware
leaves_out: Lead exposure of workers.
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access (CC0); National Palace Museum Taipei Open Data; Wikimedia Commons

name: Tin-opacified glaze
date_note: Abbasid Basra c.8th–9th c.
making_significance: Adding tin oxide made an opaque white glaze imitating Chinese porcelain, spreading from Iraq to Spain, Italy and the Netherlands.
materials_techniques: tin oxide; lead glaze; in-glaze painting
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); Rijksmuseum (public-domain images); Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access (CC0); Wikimedia Commons

name: Lustre painting on ceramics
date_note: lustre on glass in Egypt 8th c.; on ceramics in Abbasid Iraq 9th c.
making_significance: A third firing in reducing conditions leaves nanoparticles of silver and copper that give a metallic sheen.
materials_techniques: silver and copper pigments; reduction firing
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access (CC0); Wikimedia Commons

name: Celadon
other_names: greenware; Yue ware; Longquan; Goryeo cheongja
date_note: Yue wares from Eastern Han; Goryeo inlaid celadon 12th c.
making_significance: Iron-bearing glazes fired in reduction turn jade-green, prized in China, Korea and across the Indian Ocean.
materials_techniques: iron glaze; reduction firing; sanggam inlay
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access (CC0); National Museum of Korea e-museum (KOGL Type 1 where marked); National Palace Museum Taipei Open Data

name: Porcelain making
date_note: white porcelain in northern China 6th c.; Jingdezhen from Song; Meissen 1708–09
making_significance: Kaolin and porcelain stone fired to about 1300°C make a white, translucent body that other regions spent centuries trying to copy.
functions: food and storage;rule and display;exchange and value
leaves_out: Kiln workers and decorators, often unnamed.
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); National Palace Museum Taipei Open Data; Rijksmuseum (public-domain images); Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access (CC0); ColBase Japan national museums (Japan Government Standard Terms)

name: Fritware
date_note: Seljuq Iran and Fatimid–Ayyubid Egypt c.11th–12th c.; İznik 15th–17th c.
making_significance: Ground quartz with glass frit and a little clay gave Islamic potters a white body close to porcelain.
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access (CC0); Walters Art Museum (CC0)

name: Underglaze cobalt blue
date_note: cobalt on Abbasid wares 9th c.; Jingdezhen blue-and-white from c.1320s using Persian cobalt
making_significance: Cobalt painted under a clear glaze produced blue-and-white wares traded and copied from Iran to Delft to Puebla.
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); National Palace Museum Taipei Open Data; Rijksmuseum (public-domain images); Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access (CC0)

name: Overglaze enamel on ceramics
date_note: mina'i ware in Iran late 12th c.; doucai 1460s; Arita enamels 1640s
making_significance: Coloured enamels painted over a fired glaze and refired at lower temperature widened the palette of ceramics.
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access (CC0); ColBase Japan national museums (Japan Government Standard Terms); National Palace Museum Taipei Open Data

name: Raku
date_note: Chōjirō with Sen no Rikyū c.1570s–80s; Western 'raku' from c.1960 differs
making_significance: Hand-shaped tea bowls pulled red-hot from the kiln and cooled quickly, made for the tea ceremony by the Raku family line.
leaves_out: American post-firing reduction raku is a separate adaptation.
free_sources: ColBase Japan national museums (Japan Government Standard Terms); Met Open Access (CC0); Wikimedia Commons

name: Salt glaze
date_note: Rhineland (Siegburg, Raeren) c.15th c.
making_significance: Throwing salt into a hot kiln forms a thin orange-peel glaze on stoneware, used for Rhenish jugs and later English and American wares.
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); Rijksmuseum (public-domain images); Wikimedia Commons

name: Terra sigillata moulding
date_note: Arretine ware from c.40 BCE; Gaulish samian 1st–3rd c. CE
making_significance: Red gloss slip over bowls formed in stamped moulds produced standard tableware across the Roman Empire, often stamped with workshop names.
materials_techniques: fine gloss slip; decorated moulds; potter's stamps
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); Wikimedia Commons; Europeana; Archaeology Data Service (open reports)

name: Attic black-figure and red-figure
date_note: black-figure Corinth c.700 BCE; red-figure Athens c.530 BCE
making_significance: Controlling oxidising and reducing phases turned a fine iron-rich slip black against the orange body, allowing painted scenes.
leaves_out: Workshop labour, including enslaved workers.
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); Walters Art Museum (CC0); Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access (CC0); Wikimedia Commons

name: Egyptian faience
date_note: Predynastic Egypt and Mesopotamia; Harappan faience
making_significance: Ground quartz mixed with alkali forms its own glaze by efflorescence or cementation on firing, used for bright blue-green amulets and tiles.
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access (CC0); Walters Art Museum (CC0); Wikimedia Commons

name: Polychrome slip painting (Andes and Mesoamerica)
date_note: Nasca from c.100 BCE; Maya Classic 250–900 CE
making_significance: Many-coloured mineral slips burnished and fired produced painted vessels carrying mythic scenes and hieroglyphic texts.
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access (CC0); Wikimedia Commons

name: Qvevri making
date_note: wine residues in jars at Gadachrili Gora, Georgia c.6000 BCE; qvevri tradition ongoing (UNESCO 2013)
making_significance: Georgian potters coil large egg-shaped jars, lined with beeswax and buried to ferment and store wine.
free_sources: UNESCO World Heritage / Intangible Cultural Heritage pages (link out); Wikimedia Commons

name: Core-formed glass
date_note: Mesopotamia and Egypt c.1500 BCE
making_significance: Hot glass was trailed around a removable core of clay and dung, then combed into festoons, to make small vessels before blowing.
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access (CC0); Wikimedia Commons

name: Cast and cold-worked glass
date_note: Late Bronze Age; Hellenistic cast bowls
making_significance: Glass was cast in moulds or slumped over forms and then ground and polished like stone.
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access (CC0)

name: Glassblowing
date_note: Levant c.1st c. BCE; mould-blowing by 1st c. CE (e.g. Ennion)
making_significance: Inflating a gather of glass on a blowpipe made glass cheap and fast to shape, spreading it across the Roman world and beyond.
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access (CC0); Wikimedia Commons

name: Enamelled and gilded glass
date_note: Syria and Egypt late 12th–14th c.; earlier Roman examples
making_significance: Enamel and gold fired onto blown glass decorated mosque lamps, beakers and bottles later copied in Venice.
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); Walters Art Museum (CC0); Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access (CC0)

name: Cameo glass
date_note: Roman c.25 BCE–50 CE (Portland Vase); 19th-c. English revival; Qing carved glass
making_significance: Layers of differently coloured glass are cut back to leave a relief image.
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); Wikimedia Commons

name: Float glass
date_note: Pilkington, announced 1959
making_significance: Floating molten glass on molten tin made flat, even sheet glass at industrial scale for curtain walls and screens.
free_sources: Google Patents / national patent offices (public documents); Wikimedia Commons

name: Indo-Pacific drawn glass beads
date_note: Arikamedu, Mantai, Khao Sam Kaeo from c.4th c. BCE
making_significance: Drawing hollow glass tubes and cutting them made small monochrome beads by the million, traded across the Indian Ocean.
free_sources: open-access journal articles; Wikimedia Commons

name: Ile-Ife glass making
date_note: c.11th–15th c. (Babalola et al. 2017)
making_significance: Makers at Ile-Ife produced their own high-lime, high-alumina glass from local materials and made beads in quantity.
materials_techniques: primary glass making; crucibles; bead drawing
leaves_out: Refutes the assumption that African glass beads were all imported.
free_sources: open-access journal articles; Wikimedia Commons

name: Cold-hammering native copper
date_note: Çayönü, Anatolia c.8th millennium BCE; Old Copper Complex, Great Lakes c.5000–1000 BCE (some earlier)
making_significance: Native copper was hammered and annealed into awls, beads and points without smelting, in Anatolia and independently around the Great Lakes.
free_sources: Smithsonian NMNH Anthropology via Smithsonian Open Access (CC0 where marked); open-access excavation reports; Wikimedia Commons

name: Copper smelting
date_note: Belovode, Serbia c.5000 BCE; Tal-i Iblis, Iran 5th millennium; independent Andean development later
making_significance: Reducing copper ore in a hot charcoal fire produced metal from stone, a process invented more than once.
free_sources: open-access excavation reports; open-access journal articles; Wikimedia Commons

name: Arsenical copper alloying
date_note: Nahal Mishmar hoard c.3700 BCE; Andes later
making_significance: Copper with arsenic was harder and castable, used for the Nahal Mishmar hoard and later in Andean metallurgy.
leaves_out: Arsenic fumes harmed smiths.
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons; open-access excavation reports

name: Tin bronze alloying
date_note: tin bronze foil at Pločnik c.4650 BCE contested; regular use c.3000 BCE; China c.2000 BCE
making_significance: Alloying copper with about ten per cent tin produced a stronger, better-casting metal whose supply drove long-distance trade.
leaves_out: 'Bronze Age' dates differ by region.
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access (CC0); Wikimedia Commons

name: Lost-wax casting
date_note: Mehrgarh amulet c.4000 BCE (Thoury et al. 2016); Nahal Mishmar c.3700 BCE; Igbo-Ukwu 9th–10th c. CE; Benin, Chola, Newar, Muisca
making_significance: A wax model encased in clay is melted out and replaced by metal, allowing complex one-off castings.
object_types: Benin plaques; Chola bronzes; tunjos; Akan goldweights
leaves_out: Benin works looted 1897.
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access (CC0); Wikimedia Commons; British Museum EMKP (CC)

name: Piece-mould casting
date_note: Erlitou c.1700 BCE to Han
making_significance: Chinese founders cast ritual bronzes in assembled clay section-moulds, organised in large workshops such as those at Anyang.
functions: ritual and belief;rule and display;play and music
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access (CC0); National Palace Museum Taipei Open Data; Wikimedia Commons

name: Repoussé and chasing
date_note: Mesopotamia and Egypt by 3rd millennium BCE; Andean goldwork; Mississippian copper plates; Newar metalwork
making_significance: Hammering sheet metal from the back and refining from the front forms relief images and vessels.
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access (CC0); Wikimedia Commons

name: Granulation
date_note: Ur c.2500 BCE; Etruscan fine granulation 7th c. BCE
making_significance: Tiny gold spheres were fused to a gold ground by colloidal or eutectic bonding.
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); Walters Art Museum (CC0); Wikimedia Commons

name: Filigree
date_note: Mesopotamia 3rd millennium BCE; ongoing (Cuttack, Mompox)
making_significance: Fine twisted wires were soldered into openwork patterns in gold and silver.
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); Walters Art Museum (CC0); Wikimedia Commons

name: Wire drawing
date_note: earliest confirmed draw-plates 6th–8th c. CE (Old Uppsala, Vendel Period; Merovingian finds); Viking Age plates at Birka, Haithabu and Staraya Ladoga; drawn wire of Roman date claimed; earlier wire made by strip-twisting and hammering
making_significance: Pulling metal through a series of shrinking holes produced uniform wire for chain mail, jewellery and later cables.
free_sources: open-access journal articles; Wikimedia Commons
notes: Date of first draw-plate uncertain; verify.

name: Leaf gilding
date_note: Egypt Old Kingdom; ongoing (Mandalay gold beaters)
making_significance: Gold beaten into leaves thinner than paper was laid over wood, gesso and stone.
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); Wikimedia Commons

name: Fire gilding
date_note: Warring States China c.4th c. BCE; Roman
making_significance: Gold dissolved in mercury was painted on and the mercury driven off by heat, poisoning many gilders.
leaves_out: Mercury poisoning of gilders.
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access (CC0); Wikimedia Commons

name: Depletion gilding
date_note: first millennium BCE–CE in Colombia and the Isthmus; Moche also used electrochemical plating
making_significance: Gold–copper alloy objects were heated and treated with acidic plant juices to remove copper at the surface, leaving a gold-rich skin.
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access (CC0); Wikimedia Commons

name: Niello inlay
date_note: Roman from 1st c. CE; Bronze Age black inlays debated
making_significance: A black sulphide of silver or copper was fused into engraved lines in silver.
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); Walters Art Museum (CC0); Wikimedia Commons

name: Metal inlay (damascening and koftgari)
date_note: Khurasan and Mosul inlaid brass 12th–13th c.; Mughal koftgari; Toledo damascene
making_significance: Silver, gold and copper wire or sheet was hammered into engraved or cross-hatched grounds on brass or steel.
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access (CC0); Walters Art Museum (CC0)

name: Bidri
date_note: Bahmani Bidar 14th–15th c.; ongoing
making_significance: A zinc alloy cast in Bidar is inlaid with silver and blackened with a paste of soil and ammonium chloride.
materials_techniques: zinc alloy casting; silver inlay; soil blackening
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); Wikimedia Commons

name: Bloomery iron smelting
date_note: widespread by c.1200 BCE in Anatolia and the Levant; early African dates (e.g. Termit, Nsukka) debated
making_significance: Smelting iron ore below its melting point produced a spongy bloom that smiths consolidated by hammering, invented more than once.
leaves_out: Diffusion vs independent African invention is debated.
free_sources: open-access excavation reports; open-access journal articles; Wikimedia Commons

name: Blast furnace and cast iron
date_note: China c.5th c. BCE; Lapphyttan, Sweden c.1150–1350 CE
making_significance: Tall furnaces made liquid iron that could be cast in moulds; China cast iron tools and moulds at scale from the Warring States.
free_sources: open-access excavation reports; open-access journal articles; Wikimedia Commons

name: Haya preheated furnace
date_note: Schmidt and Avery (1978) dated preheated-blast smelting at KM2/KM3 (Kemondo Bay) to c. 1,500–2,000 years ago; the preheating and 'steel' claims were challenged by Rehder (1986) and Eggert (1987)
making_significance: Haya smelters in northwest Tanzania ran furnaces with preheated air blasts, reconstructed in the 1970s with elders.
materials_techniques: preheated tuyères; natural-draught and bellows furnaces
leaves_out: Reconstruction depended on Haya elders' knowledge.
free_sources: open-access journal articles; Wikimedia Commons

name: Crucible steel
date_note: South India and Sri Lanka (Kodumanal, Tissamaharama) from late 1st millennium BCE; Merv 9th–10th c.
making_significance: Iron and carbon sealed in clay crucibles produced high-carbon steel whose patterned blades were prized across West Asia.
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); open-access journal articles; Wikimedia Commons

name: Pattern welding
date_note: Roman and Migration Period swords from 2nd–3rd c.; Javanese kris pamor
making_significance: Twisting and forge-welding bars of different iron and steel produced patterned, layered blades, in Europe and in Javanese kris.
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); Wikimedia Commons; UNESCO World Heritage / Intangible Cultural Heritage pages (link out)

name: Tatara smelting
date_note: from c.6th c.; Edo-period form; still operated for tamahagane in Shimane
making_significance: A clay box furnace fed with iron sand and charcoal for three days produces tamahagane steel for Japanese swords.
free_sources: ColBase Japan national museums (Japan Government Standard Terms); Wikimedia Commons

name: High-tin bronze forging
date_note: Ban Don Ta Phet, Thailand c.4th c. BCE; Javanese gamelan gongs; Korean bangjja yugi
making_significance: Bronze with about 20–25 per cent tin, brittle when cast, is hot-forged and quenched to make resonant gongs and bowls.
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); National Museum of Korea e-museum (KOGL Type 1 where marked); Wikimedia Commons

name: Cloisonné enamel
date_note: Cypriot rings c.13th–12th c. BCE; Byzantine 9th–12th c.; Chinese jingtai 15th c.
making_significance: Enamel was fused into cells formed by thin metal strips soldered to a base.
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); Walters Art Museum (CC0); National Palace Museum Taipei Open Data

name: Champlevé enamel
date_note: La Tène red enamel; Limoges 12th–13th c.
making_significance: Enamel fills troughs carved or cast into a thick metal surface.
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); Walters Art Museum (CC0); Wikimedia Commons

name: Zinc distillation
date_note: Zawar, Rajasthan c.9th c. CE onward; industrial scale 12th–18th c.
making_significance: Rajasthani smelters used inverted retorts to condense zinc vapour, the earliest large-scale production of metallic zinc.
free_sources: open-access journal articles; Wikimedia Commons

name: Patio process
date_note: Bartolomé de Medina, Pachuca 1554; used at Potosí from 1570s
making_significance: Mixing crushed ore with mercury and salt in open patios made Spanish American silver mining vastly productive, using forced mita labour and poisoning workers.
leaves_out: Andean mitayos and enslaved workers.
free_sources: Library of Congress (public-domain items); Wikimedia Commons

name: Sericulture and silk reeling
date_note: silk fabric at Qianshanyang c.2700 BCE; silk proteins at Jiahu c.6500 BCE claimed
making_significance: Raising silkworms on mulberry and reeling continuous filament from cocoons gave China a fibre it controlled for centuries.
leaves_out: Largely women's labour.
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); National Palace Museum Taipei Open Data; Wikimedia Commons

name: Bast fibre processing
date_note: dyed wild flax fibres, Dzudzuana Cave, Georgia c.30 ka (contested); linen at Nahal Hemar c.6500 BCE
making_significance: Rotting and beating flax, hemp or ramie stems frees long fibres for spinning linen and cordage.
free_sources: open-access journal articles; Wikimedia Commons

name: Drop-spindle spinning
date_note: spindle whorls in the Neolithic Near East c.7th millennium BCE; ongoing
making_significance: A weighted spindle twists fibre into yarn, a portable technique that occupied much of many women's time.
leaves_out: Hours of spinning labour are rarely counted.
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); Wikimedia Commons

name: Spinning wheel
date_note: c.1000 CE in Asia (origins debated); Europe 13th c.; Gandhi's charkha 1920s
making_significance: Turning a wheel to spin the spindle sped yarn production and later became a political symbol in India's swadeshi movement.
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); Wikimedia Commons; Library of Congress (public-domain items)

name: Backstrap loom weaving
date_note: loom parts at Hemudu, China c.5000 BCE; ancient in the Andes and Mesoamerica; ongoing
making_significance: The weaver tensions the warp with her body, producing fine cloth on a portable loom still used from Guatemala to Laos.
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); Smithsonian NMNH Anthropology via Smithsonian Open Access (CC0 where marked); Wikimedia Commons

name: Warp-weighted loom
date_note: loom weights from Neolithic southeast Europe and Anatolia; in use in Scandinavia into the 20th c.
making_significance: An upright loom with clay or stone weights on the warp made wide woollen cloth and sails.
free_sources: open-access excavation reports; Wikimedia Commons

name: Horizontal ground loom
date_note: possible loom on a Naqada I–II bowl from Badari tomb 3802 (Petrie Museum UC9547), c. 3900–3500 BCE; used by Bedouin and Central Asian weavers today
making_significance: Warp stretched between beams pegged to the ground allows long cloth and tent strips to be woven by nomadic weavers.
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); Wikimedia Commons

name: Treadle loom
date_note: Han China depictions; Europe 11th c.
making_significance: Foot pedals lifting harnesses freed the weaver's hands and sped plain and twill weaving.
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons; open-access journal articles

name: Drawloom
date_note: Laoguanshan, Chengdu loom models c.2nd c. BCE (pattern loom; whether a drawloom proper is debated)
making_significance: A second person pulling pattern cords allowed complex repeating figured silks.
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); open-access journal articles

name: Jacquard loom
date_note: Joseph-Marie Jacquard 1804
making_significance: Punched cards selected warp threads automatically, displacing draw-boys and inspiring early computing.
leaves_out: Lyon silk workers' revolts (1831, 1834).
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); Wikimedia Commons; Google Patents / national patent offices (public documents)

name: Power loom and mechanised spinning
other_names: mechanised weaving; flying shuttle; spinning jenny; water frame; spinning mule
date_note: flying shuttle 1733 (John Kay); jenny c.1764, water frame 1769, mule 1779; power loom 1785 (Edmund Cartwright)
making_significance: Spinning machines and then steam-driven looms moved textile making into factories and undercut hand weavers in Britain and India.
leaves_out: Displaced handloom weavers in Britain and India.
free_sources: Google Patents / national patent offices (public documents); Wikimedia Commons

name: Tapestry weaving
date_note: Thutmose IV tomb tapestry c.1400 BCE; Andean tapestry tunics; Chinese kesi from Tang
making_significance: Discontinuous wefts beaten down to hide the warp let weavers build images colour by colour.
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access (CC0); National Palace Museum Taipei Open Data

name: Brocade
date_note: supplementary-weft silks by mid-1st millennium CE; earliest date depends on definition
making_significance: Extra pattern wefts, often gold or silver thread, float over a ground weave.
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access (CC0); Wikimedia Commons

name: Samite
date_note: Sasanian, Sogdian and Byzantine silks c.6th c.
making_significance: A compound twill with hidden binding warps produced the roundel silks traded across Eurasia.
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access (CC0)

name: Velvet weaving
date_note: Italian velvets 14th c.; Ottoman Bursa and Safavid velvets; earlier origins debated
making_significance: Extra warp loops woven over rods and cut form a soft pile, often patterned in gold.
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access (CC0); Rijksmuseum (public-domain images)

name: Warp ikat
date_note: depicted at Ajanta c.5th–6th c.; Yemeni ikat 10th c.; antiquity likely greater
making_significance: Warp threads are tied and dyed before weaving, so the pattern blurs slightly as it emerges.
leaves_out: The Malay word 'ikat' was adopted by Dutch scholars.
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access (CC0); Rijksmuseum (public-domain images)

name: Double ikat
date_note: patola in Gujarat by c.13th–14th c.; geringsing in Tenganan, Bali
making_significance: Both warp and weft are resist-dyed so that pattern appears only when they align, made in Patan and Tenganan.
functions: clothing and adornment;ritual and belief;exchange and value
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); Rijksmuseum (public-domain images); Wikimedia Commons

name: Jamdani
date_note: Mughal-era Dhaka muslin; UNESCO 2013
making_significance: Discontinuous supplementary wefts inlaid by hand on fine cotton make floral patterns in Bengal muslin.
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); V&A collections (link out); UNESCO World Heritage / Intangible Cultural Heritage pages (link out)

name: Narrow-strip weaving
date_note: Tellem caves, Mali c.11th c.; Asante and Ewe kente 17th–18th c.
making_significance: Long narrow strips woven on double-heddle treadle looms are sewn edge to edge into large cloths.
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); British Museum EMKP (CC); Wikimedia Commons

name: Felt making
date_note: Pazyryk felts c.4th–3rd c. BCE; earlier Bronze Age examples
making_significance: Wool matted with heat, moisture and pressure makes a dense fabric for tents, carpets and clothing without spinning or weaving.
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); Wikimedia Commons; UNESCO World Heritage / Intangible Cultural Heritage pages (link out)

name: Knotted-pile carpet weaving
date_note: Pazyryk carpet c.4th–3rd c. BCE
making_significance: Rows of wool knots tied around warp threads and clipped make a durable, patterned pile.
materials_techniques: symmetrical and asymmetrical knots; Tibetan knot
leaves_out: Child labour in some modern production.
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access (CC0); Wikimedia Commons

name: Looping and nålbinding
date_note: looped fabrics at Nahal Hemar c.6500 BCE; bilum making ongoing in Papua New Guinea
making_significance: Loops of a single thread worked with a needle or fingers make stretchy bags and garments, as in Papua New Guinean bilum.
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons; Auckland Museum Online Collection (CC BY where marked)

name: Knotting and netting
date_note: Antrea net, Finland c.8300 BCE
making_significance: Knotted nets captured fish and game and carried loads.
free_sources: open-access excavation reports; Wikimedia Commons

name: Khipu construction
date_note: Wari khipu c.600 CE; Inca khipu to 16th c.; earlier Caral example contested
making_significance: Cords spun, plied, dyed and knotted in fixed positions recorded numbers and possibly narrative for the Inca state.
materials_techniques: plying direction; knot types; colour coding
leaves_out: Khipu decipherment remains incomplete; communities still keep some khipu.
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); Wikimedia Commons

name: Coiled basketry
date_note: coiled baskets in the Great Basin and Egypt by the Holocene; ongoing
making_significance: Stitching a continuous bundle into a spiral makes watertight baskets, trays and granaries.
free_sources: Smithsonian NMNH Anthropology via Smithsonian Open Access (CC0 where marked); Met Open Access (CC0); Wikimedia Commons

name: Twined basketry
date_note: twined textile impressions at Dolní Věstonice c.26 ka; ongoing
making_significance: Pairs of weft elements twisted around warps make bags, hats and mats, including Northwest Coast spruce-root hats.
free_sources: Smithsonian NMNH Anthropology via Smithsonian Open Access (CC0 where marked); Wikimedia Commons

name: Plaiting
other_names: checker and twill plaiting; pandanus plaiting
date_note: ancient; ongoing
making_significance: Interlacing flat strips of pandanus, palm or bamboo makes mats, sails and baskets across the Pacific and Southeast Asia.
free_sources: Auckland Museum Online Collection (CC BY where marked); Te Papa Collections Online (CC BY where marked; otherwise link out); Wikimedia Commons

name: Barkcloth beating
date_note: stone beaters in southern China c.6000 BCE; Pacific tapa; Ugandan barkcloth (UNESCO 2008)
making_significance: Inner bark of mulberry and fig trees is soaked and beaten into sheets, then decorated, across the Pacific, Africa and Mesoamerica.
functions: clothing and adornment;exchange and value;ritual and belief
free_sources: Te Papa Collections Online (CC BY where marked; otherwise link out); Auckland Museum Online Collection (CC BY where marked); Met Open Access (CC0); Wikimedia Commons

name: Featherwork
date_note: Wari feather panels c.600–900; Hawaiian ʻahu ʻula; Nahua amanteca feather mosaic; Amazonian featherwork ongoing
making_significance: Feathers tied into netting or glued to backings made cloaks, headdresses and mosaics of high rank.
leaves_out: Much featherwork is sacred and restricted.
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); Te Papa Collections Online (CC BY where marked; otherwise link out); Wikimedia Commons

name: Porcupine quillwork
date_note: pre-contact; ongoing
making_significance: Flattened, dyed porcupine quills are sewn or wrapped onto hide and birchbark.
free_sources: Smithsonian NMNH Anthropology via Smithsonian Open Access (CC0 where marked); Wikimedia Commons

name: Beadwork
date_note: shell and seed beadwork ancient; glass seed-bead work expands with trade beads from 16th–19th c.; ongoing
making_significance: Sewing and weaving glass beads into garments and regalia created visual languages from Lakota to Zulu to Yoruba.
free_sources: Smithsonian NMNH Anthropology via Smithsonian Open Access (CC0 where marked); Met Open Access (CC0); Wikimedia Commons

name: Embroidery
date_note: chain-stitch silk embroidery at Mashan, China c.4th–3rd c. BCE; earlier fragmentary evidence
making_significance: Stitching thread onto a ground fabric adds pattern and image and is one of the most widespread decorative crafts.
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access (CC0); Rijksmuseum (public-domain images)

name: Opus anglicanum
date_note: approximate
making_significance: Professional London workshops embroidered silk and gold vestments using underside couching, prized by popes.
leaves_out: Women embroiderers named in few records.
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); V&A collections (link out)

name: Kantha
date_note: long-standing; ongoing
making_significance: Bengali women layer worn saris and stitch them with running stitches into quilts and wraps.
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); Wikimedia Commons

name: Sashiko and boro
date_note: Edo-period rural practice; approximate
making_significance: Running stitches reinforce and patch layered indigo cotton, turning repair into pattern.
free_sources: ColBase Japan national museums (Japan Government Standard Terms); Wikimedia Commons

name: Mola reverse appliqué
date_note: late 19th–early 20th c.
making_significance: Guna women cut through layered cotton to reveal colours below, making blouse panels.
free_sources: Smithsonian NMNH Anthropology via Smithsonian Open Access (CC0 where marked); Wikimedia Commons

name: Quilting
date_note: quilted textiles at Noin-Ula, Mongolia c.1st c. BCE; ongoing
making_significance: Layers stitched together make warm bedding and armour and have carried community designs such as Gee's Bend quilts.
free_sources: Smithsonian Open Access (CC0); Met Open Access (CC0); Library of Congress (public-domain items)

name: Mordant dyeing
date_note: madder-dyed cotton at Mohenjo-daro c.2500 BCE (as usually cited)
making_significance: Metal salts such as alum fix natural dyes to fibre and let one dye give several colours.
free_sources: open-access journal articles; Met Open Access (CC0)

name: Block printing on textiles
date_note: printed silk from Han tombs c.2nd c. BCE; Indian block prints at Fustat 13th–15th c.
making_significance: Carved wooden blocks stamp mordants, resists or dyes onto cloth in repeating patterns.
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); V&A collections (link out); Wikimedia Commons

name: Kalamkari
date_note: Coromandel painted cottons from c.15th c.; Machilipatnam and Srikalahasti ongoing
making_significance: Mordants and wax resist drawn with a kalam and dyed with madder and indigo produced the painted cottons Europe called chintz.
functions: clothing and adornment;ritual and belief;exchange and value
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); Rijksmuseum (public-domain images); V&A collections (link out)

name: Batik
date_note: Javanese canting batik documented from 17th c.; wax resist older elsewhere; UNESCO 2009
making_significance: Hot wax drawn with a canting or stamped with a cap resists dye through repeated baths.
free_sources: Rijksmuseum (public-domain images); Met Open Access (CC0); Wikimedia Commons

name: Tie-resist dyeing
date_note: Wari tie-dyed tunics c.600 CE; Shōsōin textiles 8th c.; Ajanta depictions
making_significance: Binding, stitching or folding cloth before dyeing leaves resisted patterns of dots and lines.
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); ColBase Japan national museums (Japan Government Standard Terms); Wikimedia Commons

name: Adire
date_note: late 19th c. with imported cotton shirting
making_significance: Yoruba women resist-dye cotton with cassava starch or tying before indigo dyeing.
free_sources: British Museum EMKP (CC); Wikimedia Commons

name: Bogolanfini
date_note: long-standing; ongoing
making_significance: Bamana dyers paint fermented iron-rich mud onto cloth pretreated with tannin, making dark patterns.
free_sources: British Museum EMKP (CC); Wikimedia Commons

name: Kuba raffia cut-pile and appliqué
date_note: documented from 17th c.
making_significance: Kuba women embroider cut-pile patterns into raffia cloth woven by men.
functions: clothing and adornment;ritual and belief;exchange and value
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); British Museum EMKP (CC); Wikimedia Commons

name: Indigo vat dyeing
date_note: indigo-dyed cotton at Huaca Prieta, Peru c.6,200 years ago (Splitstoser et al. 2016)
making_significance: Indigo is reduced in a fermentation vat to a soluble form that turns blue on the cloth in air.
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); ColBase Japan national museums (Japan Government Standard Terms); Wikimedia Commons

name: Tyrian purple dyeing
date_note: Minoan Crete c.18th c. BCE; Levantine production; Byzantine imperial monopoly
making_significance: Dye from thousands of murex snails per garment made purple cloth a marker of rank.
free_sources: open-access journal articles; Wikimedia Commons

name: Cochineal dyeing
date_note: Andean textiles from first millennium BCE; post-1521 export to Europe
making_significance: Dried scale insects raised on nopal cactus produce a red that became New Spain's most valuable export after silver.
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access (CC0); Wikimedia Commons

name: Wax print
date_note: Dutch mechanised imitation batik from mid-19th c.; West African market from late 19th c.
making_significance: Dutch firms industrialised resin-resist printing to imitate Javanese batik, and West African traders and wearers made it their own.
leaves_out: Designs named and adopted by West African women traders.
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons; Rijksmuseum (public-domain images)

name: Chilkat weaving
date_note: pre-contact origins; ongoing (revived late 20th c.)
making_significance: Tlingit and other Northwest Coast weavers twine mountain-goat wool and cedar bark into curvilinear formline robes without a loom beam.
free_sources: Smithsonian NMNH Anthropology via Smithsonian Open Access (CC0 where marked); community-published site

name: Diné upright-loom weaving
date_note: learned from Pueblo weavers c.17th c.; ongoing
making_significance: Diné weavers make tightly woven wool blankets and rugs on vertical looms, adapting designs for the trading-post market.
free_sources: Smithsonian NMNH Anthropology via Smithsonian Open Access (CC0 where marked); Smithsonian Open Access (CC0); Wikimedia Commons

name: Harakeke weaving
date_note: from Māori settlement of Aotearoa; ongoing
making_significance: Māori weavers prepare harakeke (New Zealand flax) fibre and finger-weave cloaks and plait baskets and mats.
materials_techniques: muka fibre; whatu finger-twining; raranga plaiting
functions: clothing and adornment;food and storage;rule and display
free_sources: Te Papa Collections Online (CC BY where marked; otherwise link out); Auckland Museum Online Collection (CC BY where marked)

name: Sadu weaving
date_note: long-standing; ongoing; UNESCO: UAE Al Sadu 2011 (Urgent Safeguarding; Representative List 2025); 'Traditional weaving of Al Sadu' Kuwait and Saudi Arabia 2020, extended with Qatar 2025
making_significance: Bedouin women weave tent dividers, bags and rugs of camel, goat and sheep hair on ground looms.
free_sources: UNESCO World Heritage / Intangible Cultural Heritage pages (link out); Wikimedia Commons

name: Mortise-and-tenon joinery
date_note: Linear Pottery wells in Germany c.5100 BCE; Hemudu, China c.5000 BCE
making_significance: A projecting tenon fitted into a cut socket joins timbers without nails.
free_sources: open-access excavation reports; Wikimedia Commons

name: Dougong bracketing
date_note: depicted from Warring States; standardised in the Yingzao Fashi (1103)
making_significance: Interlocking timber bracket sets transfer roof loads to columns and were standardised in a Song building manual.
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons

name: Kerfed bentwood boxes
date_note: pre-contact; ongoing
making_significance: A single cedar plank is kerfed, steamed and bent into four sides and sewn or pegged at the corner.
free_sources: Smithsonian NMNH Anthropology via Smithsonian Open Access (CC0 where marked); Wikimedia Commons

name: Steam-bent wood (Thonet)
date_note: Michael Thonet's patents from 1841; chair No. 14 (1859)
making_significance: Steaming solid beech and bending it in iron forms allowed chairs made from a few parts and shipped flat.
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); Wikimedia Commons

name: Lacquer (urushi and qi)
date_note: Kuahuqiao lacquered bow, China c.6000 BCE; earlier Jōmon claims
making_significance: Sap of the lacquer tree, applied in many thin cured layers, gives a hard waterproof surface for vessels, armour and furniture.
leaves_out: Urushiol causes severe skin reactions for workers.
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); ColBase Japan national museums (Japan Government Standard Terms); National Palace Museum Taipei Open Data; National Museum of Korea e-museum (KOGL Type 1 where marked)

name: Marquetry and intarsia
date_note: Italian intarsia 15th c.; Boulle marquetry 17th c.; Persian khatam; Egyptian inlay far older
making_significance: Veneers of wood, shell, bone and metal are cut and fitted into pictures and patterns on furniture.
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); Rijksmuseum (public-domain images); Walters Art Museum (CC0)

name: Wood turning
date_note: turned bowl fragment from the Warrior's Tomb, Tarquinia c. 700 BCE; 7th-c. BCE turned dishes from Anatolian tumuli and lathe pivots from Thebes (Sitry); a Mycenaean claim (c. 1400–1100 BCE) is unproven
making_significance: Rotating wood on a bow or pole lathe against a chisel produces bowls, legs and spindles.
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons; open-access excavation reports

name: Dugout canoe building
date_note: Pesse canoe, Netherlands c.8000 BCE; Dufuna canoe, Nigeria c.6000 BCE
making_significance: Hollowing a single log with fire and adzes makes a boat.
free_sources: open-access excavation reports; Wikimedia Commons

name: Lashed-lug boat building
date_note: Butuan boats c.4th–13th c. (dates vary)
making_significance: Planks edge-joined with dowels are lashed to frames through carved lugs.
free_sources: open-access journal articles; Wikimedia Commons

name: Sewn-plank boat building
date_note: Khufu ship c.2500 BCE (lashed); Ferriby boats c.2000 BCE; Indian Ocean sewn boats into the 20th c.
making_significance: Planks stitched together with coir or fibre cord made flexible hulls for the Indian Ocean and early European rivers.
free_sources: open-access excavation reports; Wikimedia Commons

name: Dhow building
date_note: nailed and sewn dhows from late 1st millennium CE; ongoing in Sur, Lamu and Gujarat
making_significance: Shipwrights build dhow hulls plank-first by eye, using teak and nails or stitching.
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons; Qatar Digital Library (licence per item; check)

name: Clinker boat building
date_note: Nydam boat c.310–320 CE; Viking ships; UNESCO 2021 (Nordic clinker boats)
making_significance: Overlapping planks riveted together form light, flexible hulls, as in Viking ships.
free_sources: UNESCO World Heritage / Intangible Cultural Heritage pages (link out); Wikimedia Commons

name: Outrigger and double-hulled canoe building
date_note: ancient; revived (Hōkūleʻa 1976)
making_significance: Pacific builders lash hulls, outriggers and crossbeams with coconut fibre to make stable voyaging craft.
free_sources: Te Papa Collections Online (CC BY where marked; otherwise link out); Auckland Museum Online Collection (CC BY where marked); Wikimedia Commons

name: Skin-on-frame boats
date_note: ancient; Thule period c.1000 CE onward; ongoing
making_significance: Arctic builders stretch sewn sea-mammal skins over lashed driftwood frames for hunting and transport boats.
free_sources: Smithsonian NMNH Anthropology via Smithsonian Open Access (CC0 where marked); Wikimedia Commons

name: Reed-bundle boats
date_note: bitumen-coated reed boat remains at As-Sabiyah, Kuwait c.5500 BCE; totora boats on Lake Titicaca ongoing
making_significance: Bundled reeds lashed together float without planks, from Neolithic Gulf boats to Uros totora craft.
free_sources: open-access excavation reports; Wikimedia Commons

name: Whakairo
date_note: from Māori settlement; ongoing
making_significance: Carvers work timber, bone and stone into meeting-house panels, canoe prows and taonga following whakapapa.
free_sources: Te Papa Collections Online (CC BY where marked; otherwise link out); Auckland Museum Online Collection (CC BY where marked)

name: Dry-stone masonry
date_note: Neolithic Orkney c.3100 BCE and earlier; Great Zimbabwe 11th–15th c.; UNESCO 2018
making_significance: Stones are fitted without mortar into walls, terraces and enclosures that drain and flex.
free_sources: UNESCO World Heritage / Intangible Cultural Heritage pages (link out); Wikimedia Commons

name: Ashlar masonry
date_note: Djoser complex, Saqqara c.2650 BCE
making_significance: Squared, dressed blocks laid in regular courses allowed monumental stone architecture.
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); Wikimedia Commons

name: Cyclopean masonry
date_note: Mycenaean
making_significance: Very large roughly shaped stones fitted without mortar formed Mycenaean citadel walls.
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons

name: Inca fitted stone masonry
date_note: approximate
making_significance: Inca masons pounded and ground stones to fit tightly without mortar, making earthquake-resistant walls.
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons; UNESCO World Heritage / Intangible Cultural Heritage pages (link out)

name: Mud brick
date_note: Levantine Pre-Pottery Neolithic c.9th millennium BCE; approximate
making_significance: Mould-made or hand-shaped sun-dried bricks of earth and straw built most houses and many cities of West Asia and Egypt.
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons; open-access excavation reports

name: Fired brick
date_note: Mesopotamia 4th millennium BCE; Indus standard ratio bricks 3rd millennium BCE
making_significance: Firing moulded bricks made durable, waterproof building units, standardised in Indus cities.
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons; open-access excavation reports

name: Rammed earth
date_note: Longshan walled towns c.2500 BCE; Maghribi tabia; Great Wall sections
making_significance: Damp earth is pounded in layers inside formwork to make walls and platforms.
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons

name: Adobe
date_note: Andean adobe before 3100 BCE (Los Morteros, Chao Valley) and c. 3500 BCE (Sechín Bajo); Pueblo puddled adobe; Spanish mould-made adobe from 16th c.
making_significance: Earth, straw and water are moulded into bricks or puddled into courses for thick, thermally stable walls.
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons; Library of Congress (public-domain items)
notes: Checked: earliest Andean adobe is Preceramic (4th millennium BCE), not 2nd millennium BCE.

name: Cob
date_note: medieval Devon and elsewhere; approximate
making_significance: Earth mixed with straw is built up in wet layers without forms and trimmed into walls.
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons

name: Sudano-Sahelian earthen building
date_note: Great Mosque of Djenné rebuilt 1906–07 on 13th-c. foundations; annual replastering ongoing
making_significance: Communities build and annually replaster mosques and houses in banco earth, using protruding timbers as scaffolding.
free_sources: UNESCO World Heritage / Intangible Cultural Heritage pages (link out); Wikimedia Commons

name: Lime plaster
date_note: Natufian lime plaster c.12th millennium BCE; 'Ain Ghazal plaster statues c.7th millennium BCE
making_significance: Burning limestone and slaking it made plaster for floors, skull modelling and statues.
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons; open-access excavation reports

name: Reinforced concrete
date_note: Joseph Monier patent 1867; Hennebique system 1892
making_significance: Steel bars embedded in concrete carry tension, making frames, slabs and shells possible.
free_sources: Google Patents / national patent offices (public documents); Wikimedia Commons

name: Mosaic
date_note: Uruk clay-cone mosaic c.3500 BCE; Gordion pebble mosaics 8th c. BCE; Hellenistic tesserae; glass wall mosaic from late antiquity
making_significance: Small units of stone, clay or glass set in mortar made durable floors and walls.
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons; Met Open Access (CC0)

name: Stucco carving
date_note: Parthian and Sasanian; Maya Classic; Abbasid Samarra
making_significance: Lime or gypsum plaster was modelled or carved wet into façades, masks and wall panels.
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); Wikimedia Commons

name: True arch and vault
date_note: mud-brick vaults in Mesopotamia and Egypt by 3rd millennium BCE; approximate
making_significance: Wedge-shaped units lock together to span openings; mud-brick vaults preceded Roman stone arches.
leaves_out: Europe-centred accounts start with Rome.
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons

name: Corbel vault
date_note: Newgrange passage tomb c.3200 BCE; Mycenaean tholoi; Maya corbel arches
making_significance: Each stone course projects a little past the one below until the gap closes.
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons

name: Masonry dome
date_note: Roman concrete domes from c.1st c. BCE; Pantheon 125 CE
making_significance: Rotating an arch forms a dome, built in concrete, brick or stone over square spaces with transitional devices.
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons

name: Squinch
date_note: Palace of Ardashir, Firuzabad c.220s CE
making_significance: An arch across the corner of a square room turns it into an octagon for a dome.
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons

name: Muqarnas
date_note: late 10th–11th c. in Iraq, Iran and North Africa
making_significance: Tiers of small niche units compose three-dimensional vaults and cornices from a geometric plan.
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); Wikimedia Commons

name: Earthen mound building
date_note: Watson Brake c.3500 BCE; Poverty Point c.1700 BCE; Cahokia c.1050 CE
making_significance: Communities moved basketloads of earth to build platform mounds, effigy mounds and ridges.
free_sources: UNESCO World Heritage / Intangible Cultural Heritage pages (link out); Wikimedia Commons

name: Snow-block construction
date_note: long-standing
making_significance: Inuit builders cut blocks of wind-packed snow with a knife and spiral them into a dome shelter.
free_sources: Smithsonian NMNH Anthropology via Smithsonian Open Access (CC0 where marked); Wikimedia Commons

name: Yurt and ger construction
date_note: long-standing; UNESCO: Mongol ger 2013; Kyrgyz and Kazakh yurts 2014, extended to Karakalpak yurts 2025
making_significance: A collapsible lattice wall, roof poles and a crown ring covered in felt make a portable house.
free_sources: UNESCO World Heritage / Intangible Cultural Heritage pages (link out); Wikimedia Commons

name: Vegetable tanning
date_note: approximate; Egyptian and Near Eastern evidence; ongoing (e.g. Fez tanneries)
making_significance: Soaking hides in tannin from bark, leaves or pods makes durable, rot-resistant leather.
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); Wikimedia Commons

name: Brain and smoke tanning
date_note: long-standing; ongoing
making_significance: Hides worked with brains and smoked become soft, washable buckskin.
free_sources: Smithsonian NMNH Anthropology via Smithsonian Open Access (CC0 where marked); Wikimedia Commons

name: Parchment making
date_note: Pergamon tradition 2nd c. BCE; earlier leather rolls in Egypt; Ethiopian parchment ongoing
making_significance: Skins are limed, stretched and scraped rather than tanned, producing a writing surface.
free_sources: Walters Art Museum (CC0); British Library (public-domain digitised items); Wikimedia Commons

name: Rawhide and parfleche
date_note: long-standing; ongoing
making_significance: Plains makers paint stiff untanned hide and fold it into cases for food and belongings.
free_sources: Smithsonian NMNH Anthropology via Smithsonian Open Access (CC0 where marked); Wikimedia Commons

name: Fish-skin working
date_note: long-standing; revived (Nanai/Hezhe, Ainu, Yup'ik)
making_significance: Salmon and other fish skins are scraped, softened and sewn into waterproof clothing and bags.
free_sources: Smithsonian NMNH Anthropology via Smithsonian Open Access (CC0 where marked); Wikimedia Commons

name: Tattooing
date_note: Ötzi c.3300 BCE; Egyptian tattooed mummies c.3000 BCE; Polynesian tatau
making_significance: Pigment inserted into skin by puncture or cutting records identity, genealogy and status.
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons; Te Papa Collections Online (CC BY where marked; otherwise link out)

name: Clay tablet and stylus
date_note: proto-cuneiform Uruk IV c.3300–3200 BCE; last dated tablet c.75 CE
making_significance: Scribes pressed wedge marks into damp clay with a cut reed, producing durable records.
leaves_out: Writing invented independently several times.
free_sources: Cuneiform Digital Library Initiative (link out); Met Open Access (CC0); Wikimedia Commons

name: Cylinder seal carving
date_note: approximate
making_significance: Engraved stone cylinders rolled on clay left repeatable images marking ownership and authority.
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); Cuneiform Digital Library Initiative (link out)

name: Papyrus making
date_note: blank roll from Hemaka's tomb c.3000 BCE; Wadi al-Jarf papyri c.2560 BCE
making_significance: Strips of papyrus pith laid crosswise and pressed bond into sheets joined into rolls.
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); Wikimedia Commons

name: Palm-leaf manuscript making
date_note: earliest surviving fragments early centuries CE; in use into the 20th c.
making_significance: Processed palm leaves are incised with a stylus and blackened, or written in ink, and strung between boards.
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons; British Library (public-domain digitised items)

name: Birch-bark writing
date_note: Gandharan Buddhist scrolls c.1st c. CE; Novgorod birch-bark letters 11th–15th c.
making_significance: Birch bark served as a writing surface for Gandharan sutras and everyday Novgorod letters.
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons; British Library (public-domain digitised items)

name: Bamboo and wooden slips
date_note: earliest surviving datable set c.433 BCE (tomb of Marquis Yi of Zeng); earlier use implied
making_significance: Strips of bamboo written in ink and bound with cord were China's main books before paper.
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons; open-access journal articles

name: Papermaking in China
date_note: Fangmatan map paper c.2nd c. BCE; Cai Lun's reported improvements 105 CE
making_significance: Macerated plant fibre formed on a screen mould made a cheap writing and wrapping sheet.
leaves_out: The Cai Lun story simplifies a longer development.
free_sources: National Palace Museum Taipei Open Data; Wikimedia Commons

name: Papermaking in the Islamic world
date_note: traditionally linked to Talas 751 (contested); Baghdad paper by c.794
making_significance: Rag-based paper spread from Central Asia to Baghdad, Cairo and al-Andalus and transformed book production.
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); Wikimedia Commons; Qatar Digital Library (licence per item; check)

name: European papermaking and watermarks
date_note: Xàtiva c.1150s; Fabriano watermarks late 13th c.
making_significance: Water-powered stamping mills and wire moulds with watermarks spread from Iberia and Italy.
materials_techniques: stamping mill; wire mould; gelatin sizing
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons; Gallica BnF (public-domain items)

name: Bark paper
date_note: Maya and Aztec codices; Otomí amate-making in San Pablito ongoing
making_significance: Fig and mulberry inner bark is boiled and beaten into sheets for codices and ritual paper.
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons; Library of Congress (public-domain items)

name: Lokta paper
date_note: long-standing; ongoing
making_significance: Bark of Daphne shrubs is cooked, beaten and formed on floating moulds for documents and prayer texts.
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons

name: Woodblock printing
date_note: Korean Dharani sutra before 751; Japanese Hyakumantō Darani 764–770; Diamond Sutra 868
making_significance: Text and image carved in relief on a block are inked and printed by rubbing, enabling mass Buddhist texts.
free_sources: International Dunhuang Programme (link out); National Museum of Korea e-museum (KOGL Type 1 where marked); Wikimedia Commons

name: Ceramic movable type
date_note: Bi Sheng c.1040s (described by Shen Kuo)
making_significance: Individual fired-clay characters were set in an iron frame for printing.
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons

name: Metal movable type (Korea)
date_note: recorded 1234; earliest surviving book Jikji 1377
making_significance: Korean printers cast bronze type in sand moulds, printing Jikji before Gutenberg.
free_sources: National Museum of Korea e-museum (KOGL Type 1 where marked); Gallica BnF (public-domain items); Wikimedia Commons

name: Metal type and press (Gutenberg)
date_note: Mainz c.1450s
making_significance: A hand mould for casting type, oil-based ink and an adapted screw press made printing in the Latin alphabet fast and repeatable.
leaves_out: Not the first movable type.
free_sources: Library of Congress (public-domain items); Gallica BnF (public-domain items); Wikimedia Commons

name: Intaglio printmaking
date_note: engraving c.1430s; etching c.1500
making_significance: Lines cut or etched into metal plates hold ink that is pressed onto damp paper.
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); National Gallery of Art Washington Open Access (CC0); Rijksmuseum (public-domain images)

name: Lithography
date_note: Alois Senefelder 1796
making_significance: Printing from a flat greased stone let artists draw directly for print and made colour posters possible.
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); National Gallery of Art Washington Open Access (CC0); Library of Congress (public-domain items)

name: Letterpress
date_note: Stanhope iron press c.1800; steam press 1814; craft revival late 20th c.
making_significance: Relief type printed on iron and steam presses produced newspapers and posters, later revived as craft.
free_sources: Library of Congress (public-domain items); NYPL Digital Collections (public-domain items)

name: Photography
date_note: Niépce c.1826–27; daguerreotype and calotype 1839
making_significance: Light-sensitive materials fixed camera images, changing how objects, people and places were recorded and reproduced.
free_sources: Library of Congress (public-domain items); National Gallery of Art Washington Open Access (CC0); Rijksmuseum (public-domain images)

name: Offset lithography
date_note: Ira Rubel 1904; others
making_significance: Ink transferred from a plate to a rubber blanket then to paper allowed fast, cheap colour printing.
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons; Library of Congress (public-domain items)

name: Screen printing
date_note: stencil precursors (e.g. katazome) older; silk-screen patent 1907
making_significance: Ink forced through a mesh stencil prints flat colour on paper, textiles and objects.
free_sources: MoMA collection (link out; metadata CC0); Library of Congress (public-domain items); Wikimedia Commons

name: CNC machining
date_note: MIT numerically controlled milling 1952
making_significance: Coded instructions drive cutting machines, linking digital design to physical making.
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons

name: 3D printing
date_note: Hideo Kodama 1981; Charles Hull stereolithography patent 1984–86
making_significance: Objects are built layer by layer from digital files, enabling distributed and custom making.
free_sources: Google Patents / national patent offices (public documents); Wikimedia Commons

name: Laser cutting
date_note: Western Electric 1965
making_significance: A focused laser cuts or engraves sheet materials from digital drawings.
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons

name: Semiconductor photolithography
date_note: planar process and integrated circuits 1959; ongoing (Taiwan, Korea)
making_significance: Light-patterned layers on silicon wafers make the integrated circuits in every digital device.
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons; NASA imagery (US public domain)

name: Fresco
date_note: Aegean wall painting c.1700 BCE (true fresco debated); Roman; Italian Renaissance
making_significance: Pigments in water painted into wet lime plaster become part of the wall as it sets.
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons; Met Open Access (CC0)

name: Egg tempera
date_note: Byzantine icons from c.6th c.; Ethiopian icons
making_significance: Pigments bound in egg yolk on gessoed panels dry fast and allow fine hatched modelling.
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); Walters Art Museum (CC0); National Gallery of Art Washington Open Access (CC0)

name: Oil painting
date_note: Bamiyan murals 7th c. with drying-oil binders; Netherlandish oil painting 15th c.
making_significance: Pigments ground in drying oils allowed slow blending and glazes; earliest known use is in Bamiyan, not Flanders.
leaves_out: Europe-centred origin story.
free_sources: National Gallery of Art Washington Open Access (CC0); Rijksmuseum (public-domain images); Met Open Access (CC0); SMK National Gallery of Denmark (CC0)

name: Encaustic
date_note: Greek sources; Fayum portraits 1st–3rd c. CE
making_significance: Pigments in hot beeswax were applied to wood panels, as in Roman-Egyptian mummy portraits.
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); Wikimedia Commons

name: Persianate and Mughal miniature painting
date_note: Ilkhanid Iran c.1300; Safavid, Ottoman, Mughal and Rajput workshops; ongoing
making_significance: Workshop artists ground mineral pigments, painted in layers on burnished paper and signed collaborative pages.
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access (CC0); Walters Art Museum (CC0); Staatliche Museen zu Berlin SMB-digital (CC BY-SA where marked)

name: Qalam calligraphy
date_note: proportioned scripts attributed to Ibn Muqla, 10th c.
making_significance: Calligraphers cut reed pens at precise angles and wrote according to proportional systems based on the rhombic dot.
materials_techniques: reed pen; carbon ink; burnished paper
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access (CC0); Walters Art Museum (CC0)

name: Ink stick and brush
date_note: carbon inks earlier; moulded ink cakes by Han
making_significance: Soot bound with animal glue into sticks is ground on a stone and used with animal-hair brushes for writing and painting.
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); National Palace Museum Taipei Open Data; ColBase Japan national museums (Japan Government Standard Terms)

name: Lacquer painting
date_note: maki-e from Nara–Heian; Vietnamese sơn mài developed 1930s
making_significance: Metal powders or pigments are sprinkled or painted into wet lacquer and polished.
free_sources: ColBase Japan national museums (Japan Government Standard Terms); Met Open Access (CC0)

name: Thangka painting
date_note: c.11th c.; ongoing
making_significance: Painters grid sacred proportions on sized cotton and apply mineral pigments to make portable devotional images.
free_sources: Himalayan Art Resources (link out); Met Open Access (CC0); Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access (CC0)

name: Bark painting
date_note: long-standing; ongoing; commercial form from 20th c.
making_significance: Artists paint ochres onto flattened stringybark with fine brushes, often in rarrk cross-hatching.
leaves_out: Ownership of designs belongs to clans.
free_sources: community-published site; Trove National Library of Australia (link out; public-domain items where marked)

name: Acrylic dot painting (Western Desert)
date_note: Papunya 1971
making_significance: Western Desert artists translated ground and body designs into acrylic on board and canvas.
leaves_out: Some early works disclosed restricted designs.
free_sources: community-published site

name: Stick charts
date_note: long-standing; described by outsiders from the 19th c.
making_significance: Marshallese navigators lashed sticks and shells to model ocean swell patterns and islands.
free_sources: Smithsonian NMNH Anthropology via Smithsonian Open Access (CC0 where marked); Wikimedia Commons

name: Star compass wayfinding
date_note: ancient; revived by Mau Piailug and Nainoa Thompson from 1976
making_significance: Navigators hold a mental compass of star rising and setting points, swells and birds to cross open ocean.
free_sources: community-published site; Wikimedia Commons

name: Astrolabe making
date_note: Greek theory; early Islamic makers 8th c.; earliest surviving dated examples 10th c.
making_significance: Engraved brass plates and a rete model the sky for time-telling and astronomy.
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); Wikimedia Commons

name: Agricultural terracing
date_note: approximate; many independent traditions; Andean, Yemeni, Ifugao and Hani terraces
making_significance: Stepped, walled fields hold soil and water on steep slopes.
leaves_out: Ifugao terrace ages debated.
free_sources: UNESCO World Heritage / Intangible Cultural Heritage pages (link out); Wikimedia Commons

name: Chinampas
date_note: approximate; Xochimilco chinampas ongoing
making_significance: Plots built from lake mud and vegetation between canals made the Basin of Mexico highly productive.
free_sources: UNESCO World Heritage / Intangible Cultural Heritage pages (link out); Wikimedia Commons

name: Budj Bim eel aquaculture
date_note: channels dated c.6,600 years ago; Budj Bim Cultural Landscape inscribed as World Heritage 2019 (not an ICH element)
making_significance: Gunditjmara people shaped lava-flow channels, weirs and ponds to trap and hold eels.
free_sources: community-published site; UNESCO World Heritage / Intangible Cultural Heritage pages (link out)

name: Qanat
date_note: aflaj at Hili 15 and Bida Bint Saud (UAE) associated with Iron Age II pottery c. 1000–600 BCE; Iranian origin argued (English, Lightfoot), Arabian origin argued (Al Tikriti); secure absolute dates lacking (Charbonnier)
making_significance: Gently sloping tunnels bring groundwater to fields and towns by gravity.
free_sources: UNESCO World Heritage / Intangible Cultural Heritage pages (link out); Wikimedia Commons

name: Cultural burning
date_note: deep antiquity; ongoing; term 'fire-stick farming' coined by Rhys Jones 1969
making_significance: Aboriginal land managers use frequent low-intensity fire to shape vegetation and reduce fuel.
leaves_out: Indigenous knowledge suppressed under colonisation.
free_sources: community-published site

name: Amazonian dark earth
date_note: c.500 BCE onward; approximate
making_significance: Charcoal, pottery and organic waste built persistent fertile soils along Amazonian rivers.
free_sources: open-access journal articles

name: Kintsugi
date_note: Muromachi period, c.15th–16th c.; approximate
making_significance: Broken ceramics are rejoined with urushi lacquer and dusted with gold, displaying the repair.
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); ColBase Japan national museums (Japan Government Standard Terms)

name: Darning
date_note: long-standing
making_significance: Weaving new threads across a hole restores worn textiles.
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons

name: Visible mending
date_note: contemporary movement c.2010s
making_significance: Menders make repairs deliberately visible as a stance against disposable consumption.
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons

name: Mesoamerican rubber processing
other_names: rubber from latex and morning glory
date_note: Paso de la Amada balls c.1600 BCE; El Manatí balls earlier; Hosler et al. 1999
making_significance: Mixing Castilla elastica latex with morning-glory juice produced bouncing rubber for ballgame balls.
free_sources: open-access journal articles; Wikimedia Commons

name: Vulcanisation
date_note: Charles Goodyear patent 1844; Thomas Hancock (UK) 1843
making_significance: Heating rubber with sulphur made it stable, enabling tyres, hoses and footwear and a global demand for latex.
leaves_out: Demand drove forced rubber collection in Congo and Amazonia.
free_sources: Google Patents / national patent offices (public documents); Wikimedia Commons

name: Interchangeable parts
date_note: Honoré Blanc 1785; US armouries 1820s; standardised Qin crossbow triggers 3rd c. BCE as earlier parallel
making_significance: Making parts to gauges so any part fits any product enabled mass production and repair by replacement.
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons

name: Moving assembly line
date_note: Ford Highland Park 1913
making_significance: Moving work past fixed workers cut assembly times and deskilled factory labour.
leaves_out: Line workers' experience.
free_sources: Library of Congress (public-domain items); Wikimedia Commons

name: Injection moulding
date_note: Hyatt brothers 1872; screw injection 1946
making_significance: Molten plastic forced into steel moulds makes identical parts in seconds, the basis of plastic consumer goods.
free_sources: Google Patents / national patent offices (public documents); Wikimedia Commons
